sections.body:
Asking for help means telling somebody that you need something they can give you. It is a skill, like tying your shoes or reading. Children who practise it get what they need faster.

Some children think asking is weak. It is not. A child who asks a clear question has already done half the work. The other half, the doing, is easier with help.

Asking is hard in two moments. The first is when something is new and you are shy. The second is when you are cross, because anger makes people avoid asking. Both moments pass faster when you have the words ready.

Good asking has three parts: **what is wrong**, **what you need**, and **who you are asking**. "The tap is leaking and I need a cloth, please" is a complete request. "Help!" is not, and it makes the other person guess.

And help does not always come from a grown-up. A friend can help. A teacher can help. Even a pet can help, by sitting quietly next to you while you tell somebody else what happened.
examples: The tap is leaking and I need a cloth.
I cannot reach the top shelf.
sections.heading: Asking for help is a skill

sections.body:
Some things you can carry on your own for a while. Some things you tell a grown-up about right now. Here is how to tell them apart.

Try it yourself first when the problem is small and safe. A loose shoelace. A book that fell down. A puzzle piece in the wrong place. Trying first is good practice, and it teaches you what you can do.

Ask quickly when you are stuck. Stuck is not the same as failed. Getting help after two tries is smart, not lazy.

Tell an adult straight away when somebody is hurt, when you are lost, or when a grown-up is doing something that worries you. You never have to be sure first. Tell them anyway.

Always tell an adult if somebody asks you to keep a secret that feels wrong, if somebody touches you in a way you do not like, or if you feel scared and you do not know why. Those are the secrets that are not yours to keep. It is never tattling to tell an adult about these things.

Notice the difference. Small problem: solve it or ask for a hand. Big worry: tell a grown-up today, not next week.
examples: I tried twice and I am stuck.
I need to tell you something that feels wrong.
I cannot find my mum and I feel scared.
sections.heading: When you should ask straight away

sections.body:
When you need help, these five steps make it easier for the other person and for you.

One. Come close. Walk to the person. Do not shout from across the room. Standing near tells them you are talking to them.

Two. Say what is wrong. One clear sentence. "My shoelace came off." "I do not understand this question."

Three. Say what you need. This is the part people forget. "I need a hand." "I need to read it to you." "I need you to come with me."

Four. Listen. The answer may not be the answer you wanted. That is okay. Listen anyway, because the next step depends on it.

Five. Try again if it did not work. Ask another person. Say it a different way. Say, "She cannot help me. Can you?" That is not rude. It is practical.

And one more habit: say thank you when the help comes. And tell the person it worked, so they know they did a good job.
examples: I need you to come with me.
She cannot help me. Can you help me?
sections.heading: How to ask for help in five steps
steps: Walk close to the person you are asking.
Say what is wrong in one sentence.
Say what kind of help you need.
If it did not work, ask somebody else.

sections.body:
These are the words for asking for help. Learn them and you can ask clearly in any situation.

Help is what you need from somebody else. You can ask for help with a task, with a feeling, or with a person.

To **ask for help** means to say out loud that you need it. It is not the same as complaining.

A **grown-up** is an adult who looks after children: a parent, a teacher, a family friend, a school nurse. Grown-ups are used to being asked.

Try first means you make a small attempt before you ask. It is not a test you can fail. Trying first is how you learn what you can do on your own.

Say each word out loud, then use one of them with a real person today.
examples: Can you give me some help?
I am going to ask for help.
I told a grown-up straight away.
sections.heading: The help words, one by one

terms.example: I need some help with this.
terms.gloss: What you need from somebody else. You can need help with a task, a feeling or a person.

terms.example: I asked for help and she came straight away.
terms.gloss: To say out loud that you need it. It is not the same as complaining.

terms.example: I told a grown-up about it.
terms.gloss: An adult who looks after children, like a parent, a teacher or the school nurse.

terms.example: I tried first, and then I asked.
terms.gloss: To make a small attempt before you ask for help.

sections.body:
Sometimes you ask, and the person says no, or they say something unhelpful like "just try again". That happens. Here is what to do next.

Try the next person. There is almost always somebody else. Another child, another teacher, a friend's mum. Asking twice is not rude.

Say it in another way. Sometimes the person did not understand you. "I need help with the scissors" is clearer than "come here".

Write it down. If you cannot say it out loud, write it on paper or draw it. Show that to the person.

Ask a bigger person. If the small things do not work, go up. Ask the head teacher or the school nurse. Adults are there for exactly this.

Do not blame yourself. Sometimes help does not come. That is not your fault, and it does not mean you asked wrongly. It means the person was busy or did not listen.

Do something small meanwhile. Sit somewhere safe, drink some water, breathe, hold a soft toy. You can wait for help while looking after yourself.
examples: I need help with the scissors, please.
I will write it down instead of saying it.
Can I ask the head teacher?
sections.heading: If the first person cannot help

sections.body:
Most problems can wait until you are ready to ask. A few things never wait.

Tell a grown-up straight away if somebody hurts you or you hurt somebody. Tell them if you are lost, or if a grown-up makes you feel scared or unsafe.

Tell them if somebody asks you to keep a secret that feels strange inside. A good adult will not ask a child to keep a secret like that.

Tell them if somebody touches you in a way you do not like, or asks you to touch them. You never have to be polite about this one.

Tell them if you feel very unwell, or if you are being bullied again and again.

If you are not sure whether something counts, tell a grown-up anyway. They would rather check and find nothing than check late. And if the first adult does not help, tell another one. Keep telling until somebody helps.
examples: Somebody touched me and I did not like it.
I am lost and I cannot find my mum.
I do not like this secret.
sections.heading: Some things you always tell an adult about

item.summary: Asking for help is a skill, not a weakness. After reading this, you can try first, ask clearly, say what kind of help you need, and tell a grown-up straight away when something is really wrong.
item.title: How to Ask for Help
